title: Divisibility
short: a ∣ b means b = ak for some integer k; if a divides b and c, it divides every combination mb + nc.
trouble: Students read a ∣ b as the fraction a/b, or reverse the roles: 3 ∣ 12 is true, but 12 ∣ 3 is false.

blocks.html: Number theory is the study of the integers $\dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots$ and of the patterns hidden in them. Its first and most basic idea is one you met in grade 6, when you listed factors: one whole number dividing another with nothing left over. Here we make that idea exact, so that we can prove things about it.

Definition. For integers $a$ and $b$, we say $a$ divides $b$, and write $a \mid b$, when there is an integer $k$ with $b = ak$. Then $a$ is a divisor (or factor) of $b$, and $b$ is a multiple of $a$. When no such $k$ exists we write $a \nmid b$.

items: $-4 \mid 20$, because $20 = (-4)(-5)$. Signs never change whether one number divides another.
$0 \nmid 5$: the only multiple of $0$ is $0$ itself.

blocks.html: Notice that $a \mid b$ is a statement, true or false. It is not a number, and it is not the fraction $a/b$. The fraction $12/3$ equals $4$; the statement $3 \mid 12$ is simply true.

blocks.text: Rules that follow from the definition

items: Transitive: if $a \mid b$ and $b \mid c$, then $a \mid c$.
Combinations: if $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$, then $d \mid (ma + nb)$ for all integers $m$ and $n$. In particular $d$ divides $a + b$ and $a - b$.
Size: if $a \mid b$ and $b \neq 0$, then $|a| \le |b|$, since $|b| = |a|\,|k|$ with $|k| \ge 1$.

blocks.html: Each rule has a two-line direct proof: rewrite every "divides" as an equation, then factor. For combinations, suppose $a = dk$ and $b = dl$. Then $$ma + nb = mdk + ndl = d(mk + nl),$$ and $mk + nl$ is an integer, so $d \mid (ma + nb)$. Transitivity works the same way: $b = ak$ and $c = bl$ give $c = a(kl)$. This "write it as an equation" move is how almost every proof in this course begins.

blocks.title: Divisors of two numbers at once
blocks.q: Suppose a positive integer $d$ divides both $n$ and $n + 15$. Which values can $d$ have?
steps: By the combination rule, $d$ divides the difference $(n + 15) - n = 15$.
So $d$ is a positive divisor of $15$: $d \in \{1, 3, 5, 15\}$.
Each one really occurs: take $n = 15$, which works for all four.

blocks.title: A short proof
blocks.q: Show that if $n$ is odd, then $8 \mid n^{2} - 1$.
steps: One of $k$ and $k + 1$ is even, so $k(k + 1) = 2j$ for an integer $j$.

blocks.html: Reading $a \mid b$ as the fraction $a/b$, or swapping the roles. $3 \mid 12$ is true, but $12 \mid 3$ is false. Say it aloud as "$a$ divides $b$", then ask: is $b$ a multiple of $a$? The divisor is on the left, and (unless $b = 0$) it is never larger in size than $b$.
$a \mid b$ means $b = ak$ for some integer $k$. Divisibility survives sums, differences and multiples: if $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$, then $d \mid ma + nb$.
